examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Coefficient in a Second-Degree Taylor Polynomial
examples.problem: What is the coefficient of $(x+2)^2$ in the second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}$ at $x = -2?$
examples.worked_solution:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=-2$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x)=f(-2)+{f}^{′}(-2)(x+2)+\frac{{f}^{″}(-2)}{2}(x+2)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of $(x+2)^2$ in the above Taylor polynomial is 

$$
\dfrac{f''(-2)}{2}.
$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative $f''(x)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\eqalign{
		f(x)&=\dfrac{1}{x}\
		f'(x)&=-\dfrac{1}{x^2}\
		f''(x)&=\dfrac{2}{x^3}
		
	}
$$

Then, we evaluate $f''(x)$ at $x=-2.$ This gives

$$
f''(-2)=\dfrac{2}{(-2)^3}=-\dfrac{1}{4}.
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of $(x+2)^2,$ as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
	\dfrac{f''(-2)}{2}&=\dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)}{2}=-\dfrac{1}{8}.
}
$$

feedback.problem:
Find the second-degree Taylor polynomial ${P}_{2}(x)$ of $f(x)=\frac{4}{x}$ about $x=2.$

${P}_{2}(x)=$
{{field-1}}$\,-$
{{field-2}}$(x-2)\,+$
{{field-3}}${(x-2)}^{2}$
feedback.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=2,$ we plug $a=2$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(2)+{f}^{′}(2)(x-2)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(2){(x-2)}^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(2),$ ${f}^{′}(2),$ and ${f}^{″}(2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{4}{x} & ⟹ &  & f(2) & =2 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{4}{{x}^{2}} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(2) & =-1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{8}{{x}^{3}} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(2) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(2),$ ${f}^{′}(2),$ and ${f}^{″}(2)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =2+(-1)(x-2)+1\cdot \frac{1}{2}{(x-2)}^{2} \\  & =2-1(x-2)+\frac{1}{2}{(x-2)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
